diagnostic_evidence.quote: A sufficient condition for the width to ensure injectivity of the encoder is $n_\ell \geq n_\text{in}$, for $\ell = 1,\ldots, L-1$.

issues.failure_explanation: Nondecreasing layer widths do not by themselves make a neural-network layer injective; injectivity depends on weights and activation functions. Moreover, the cited universal approximation theorem gives only finite-width epsilon-approximation of continuous functions, not exact injectivity, not \Varepsilon_1=0, and not a limit as the total number of trainable weights tends to infinity with fixed width.

failure_location.quote: To ensure the injectivity of the encoder approximated by a neural network, each layer must be injective, condition which is satisfied when $n_\ell \geq n_{\ell-1}$ for all hidden layers, so $n_\ell \geq n_\text{in}$ for $\ell = 1,\ldots,L-1$. By \Cref{th:uap}, we have that $n_\ell = n_\text{in}+n_\text{out}$ is sufficient to satisfy $\Varepsilon_1 = 0$ and $\lim_{|\myw|\to\infty}\Varepsilon_2 = 0$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must replace the width-only exact-injectivity claim with an explicit injective-network construction or weaken the conclusion to approximate representation error.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised sufficient architectural condition for null representation error and the associated guideline that width alone guarantees injectivity are unreliable.
issues.title: Width condition claimed to ensure exact injectivity is unsupported
issues.why_classification: The central guarantee type (width ensuring exact injectivity/null representation error) changes; the source provides no argument that finite neural networks exactly realize the required injective maps.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We recalling that $J_{\Psi}J_{\Psi'}$ is a projection, indeed $(J_{\Psi}J_{\Psi'})(J_{\Psi}J_{\Psi'}) = J_{\Psi}(J_{\Psi'}J_{\Psi})J_{\Psi'} = J_{\Psi}J_{\Psi'}$.

issues.failure_explanation: Even for an orthogonal projection P=J_{\Psi}J_{\Psi'}, the nonzero eigenvalues of P\Lambda are generally not eigenvalues of \Lambda. For example, with \Lambda=diag(-1,-3) and P projecting onto the vector (1,1), P\Lambda has a nonzero eigenvalue -2. For non-symmetric stable \Lambda, P\Lambda can have eigenvalues with larger real part. Thus the inferred FE timestep bound is unsupported.

failure_location.quote: Due to the specific assumptions made in the construction of the decoder, the projection sets some eigenvalues to zero while leaving the others unchanged.
